caseStudyHeader.heading: Javelin Program
caseStudyHeader.body: A 12-week design thinking coaching program for IBM's top 80 client account teams.

summary.title: Outcome
summary.description: The program influenced 1.2B in revenue and trail blazed design thinking in the sales context and remains a template for similar efforts.

summary.title: Goal
summary.description: The coaching program needed to contextualize design thinking for consultants to differentiate them throughout the sales cycle.

summary.title: Role
summary.description: I was a service designer, facilitator, and coach working with a small design team. My biggest contribution to the project developing learning objectives, habits, and onboarding sales teams.

summary.title: Client and scope
summary.description: The internal client was the IBM Global Markets SVP of Integrated Accounts and my role on this team lasted just under 2 years between 2017 and 2019.

context.statement: How might we design a better way for account sellers to differentiate IBM in the sales cycle?
list: IBM's adoption of design thinking reached across the company except sales, even as client engagements showed it could impact sales performance.
Changing markets pushed sellers toward new, design-led ways of working, leading the new Enterprise Design Thinking for Sellers team to form the Javelin Program.
To teach sellers design thinking, the program's format had to fit how they actually worked.
Our vision focused on four core seller jobs, enabled by Enterprise Design Thinking.

showcases.captionBody: Sellers join the program, learn the design thinking approach, and identify a client goal.

images.alt: A collage from the program: a cheering group in a workshop room, people adding sticky notes to a wall, and a video call with a shared whiteboard.

showcases.captionBody: Sellers advance their client goal, apply design thinking, and set behavior-change goals.
Over 8 weeks, coaches help sellers progress their client goal and develop new behaviors.
Teams reflect on their progress and set goals they own moving forward.

subsections.subhead: A design decision we made was to close the distance between learning and use

showcases.captionTitle: The Client Goal made it real
showcases.captionBody: It was identified during onboarding, explored in the workshop, and advanced through remote coaching.

images.alt: A workshop slide with two Client Goal examples: a police department that needs a better way to deliver real-time information to officers in the field, and a financial services company that needs to grow how many customers use cashless payments.

showcases.captionBody: Our understanding of seller workflows let us tailor design thinking activities and mindsets to their daily work.

images.alt: A diagram titled "Opportunity entry points", grouping where sales opportunities begin: pushes, pulls, trusted partnerships and influencers.
A workshop slide titled "Frame the problem space", with As-is and To-be columns and key activities such as problem statements and empathy maps.

subsections.subhead: A design decision we made was to set a big goal and break it into effortless steps

showcases.captionBody: Coaches created a zone of proximal development by removing barriers and modeling the behaviors in practice.

images.alt: A video call with one participant laughing in the main window, four more in a row above, and notes on key habits in the chat panel.

showcases.captionBody: Focusing on one key behavior set a clear priority and prevented overwhelm, while tracking improved adoption through self-regulation.

images.alt: Two people at a whiteboard pointing to a hand-drawn radar chart and a habits timeline marked in two-week steps, surrounded by sticky-note maps.

showcases.captionBody: Every habit needs a prompt. We helped sellers identify the right moments, clarifying when to act, not just what to do.

images.alt: A flip-chart sheet titled "Restlessly re-invent sales cycle", with sticky notes in Japanese and English grouped by sales stage and red voting dots on the top issues.

subsections.subhead: A design decision we made was to scale by using existing organizational supports

showcases.captionBody: The badging platform bootstrapped sellers during the program and provided a pathway for growth after the program.

images.alt: Five IBM Enterprise Design Thinking badges: Practitioner, Co-Creator, Coach, Advocate and Leader.

showcases.captionBody: A global coaching network and cohort leaders embedded within each region were the backbone of our program.

images.alt: A group of people posing and waving in front of an IBM Studios sign.

process.statement: The biggest challenge was scaling the program worldwide.
process.description: This was challenging because I needed to develop a compelling narrative to secure stakeholder buy-in from the CMO. I then conducted and applied user research to rebuild the pilot, adapting the design thinking framework for sellers and creating a program that could scale worldwide.

outcomes.quote: For us this is more about culture and methods than about process. It helps us to change the DNA of our team towards client centricity.
outcomes.attribution: IBM Managing Director, European car manufacturer
list: Design thinking had reached every part of IBM except sales
I built the learning objectives and habits that fit how sellers actually work
We coached IBM's top 80 client account teams over a 12-week program
The program influenced $1.2B in revenue and remains a template for similar efforts
